from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES', len(reader.pages))
print('METADATA', reader.metadata)
out = Path('tmp/pdfs')
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
texts=[]
for n,p in enumerate(reader.pages,1):
    text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    (out/f'page-{n:02d}.txt').write_text(text)
    texts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {n} =====\\n\\n{text}')
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

strengths: L4Q addresses a relevant NLP deployment problem. Quantizing the combined pretrained weights and low-rank updates produces a single quantized weight path at inference while avoiding QA-LoRA’s restrictions on adapter structure.

The empirical coverage is substantial: models from 3B to 33B parameters, 3-bit and 4-bit quantization, seven commonsense tasks, and zero-/five-shot MMLU. Reported improvements recur across architectures; for example, 3-bit LLaMA-2 7B commonsense accuracy improves from QAT-LoRA’s 57.4 to 61.3.

The paper measures practical costs alongside accuracy. Reported 7B training memory falls from 79.5 GB for full QAT to 25.4 GB for L4Q, and inference measurements demonstrate benefits from merging adapters. Detailed task results and initialization, rank, and group-size ablations provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: Baseline fidelity needs clarification. Section 4.1 states that adapters receive random-A/zero-B initialization, which conflicts with LoftQ’s defining SVD-based initialization unless a subsequent initialization stage is omitted from the description. QLoRA and LoftQ also use modified uniform quantization. These disclosed variants support a restricted comparison, but superiority over the original methods remains unestablished, particularly given LoftQ’s near-chance 3-bit MMLU results.

Training-efficiency comparisons are insufficiently controlled. Appendix D gives only L4Q’s 33B model a context length of 128 instead of 2048, confounding its memory and training-time comparisons. L4Q also receives 25K iterations versus 50K for PTQ-based methods; one training-loss curve does not establish equivalent convergence or generalization. Matched-context measurements and explicit token/update budgets are needed. Appendix E additionally shows substantially higher training memory than QLoRA: 25.4 versus 7.9 GB at 7B.

The custom backward equations are not dimensionally explicit about clipping. In Equations 29–30, the condition concerns individual full-weight entries, whereas the resulting adapter gradients have different dimensions. With weight gradient G and clipping mask M, the expressions should be alpha B^T(M ⊙ G) and alpha(M ⊙ G)A^T. This may be a notation problem, but implementation evidence is needed. Moreover, QAT-LoRA’s parameters already interact through their shared loss, so the claimed absence of joint optimization is overstated.

Important reproduction details remain unresolved despite the extensive appendices. Figure 3 reports 100 training steps while Appendix B reports 12,800 iterations; gradient accumulation could explain this, but microbatch and optimizer-step counts are unspecified. LoRA scaling, complete baseline configurations, and executable details of the memory-saving backward pass are also missing. Links to underlying frameworks do not resolve these implementation-dependent uncertainties.

Several advantages over the strongest baseline are only tenths of a percentage point, without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. Superiority is also not universal: 3-bit LLaMA-2 13B obtains 50.0 on five-shot MMLU versus QLoRA’s 50.6. The substantial empirical coverage makes this close to Findings, but baseline fidelity, implementation clarity, and controlled efficiency measurements remain necessary for a confident positive recommendation.
